newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels in contact with foreign mining firms.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels in contact with foreign mining firms.

text.p: Rebels fighting to overthrow Zaire's government on Tuesday said they had been in contact with all foreign companies owning mining rights in their territory.
"We are now in contact with all the companies who have concessions here and other companies who are interested in coming here as well," rebel leader Laurent Kabila told Reuters.
Kabila heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), which launched a guerrilla war last October and now controls much of eastern Zaire.
Substantial mineral reserves, mostly of gold, lie in the 600 km (400 mile) stretch of eastern Zaire.
But Kabila said reports of preparations for a counter offensive promised by President Mobutu Sese Seko had made the mining companies wary of coming to Zaire for further discussions.

"The military pressure in Kisangani and Kalemie has made these companies wary of coming here, but we want them to come and the soil is ours. We will sell our mines to whoever can offer their services," Kabila said.

Despite potential mineral wealth which could have made it one of Africa's richest countries, Zaire has been impoverished by years of neglect, corruption and outbreaks of political and ethnic violence which have scared off potential investors.
Under rebel control are the Kimin gold mine which is part of the OKIMO concession, 84 km (50 miles) North of Bunia, and the Sominki gold concession at Kamituga, West of Bukavu.
Kimin's 2,000 sq km concession is controlled by a Belgian- Canadian consortium.
Rights to explore and exploit the rest of the 83,000 sq km OKIMO concession have been held since last year by Barrick Gold Corporation, which has spoken of investing $350 million in the area.
The Sominki at Kamituga concession is owned by an Anglo- Canadian consortium of Cluff Mining and Banro Resources Corp.
Both Kimin and Sominki were looted by soldiers of the retreating Zaire army.
"There has certainly been some damage although much is left intact. My own soldeirs have been given special instructions to keep the mines in good condition," said Kabila.

He said proceeds from gold mining could be used to fund the war and to pay the wages of the local administration in the 600 km (400 mile) slice of territory held by the rebels along the border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.

Potentially more profitable than gold are the copper and cobalt mines of the southern Shaba region which were Zaire's main export earner until political violence, lack of investment and a mine collapse decimated production in the early 1990s.
Zaire's most important source of hard currency is currently the export of diamonds from the central Kasai region and northeastern area around Kisangani, as well as stones smuggled from Angola.
Zaire's war, the latest on the world's poorest continent, was sparked off by Zairean attempts to expel back to Rwanda the Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis, a land they migrated from up to 200 years ago.
